body: The box arrived with a bag of curtains and most of what is in it is paperbacks. A wet Tuesday morning in a charity shop, and the woman going through the box is about sixty-five. Near the bottom there is a hymnbook, the small kind, with a cracked spine, initials on the flyleaf in fountain pen and a date from before she was born. Several pages have pencil against them. One corner has been turned down so often that it no longer lies flat. She does not read music and does not know the hymn. She prices it, puts it in the window with the vases, and thinks about it again on the bus home.

Somebody had used that book. Not admired it — used it, on particular Sundays in a particular year, and had gone back to one page far more often than to any of the others, which is a thing you can still see with the book shut.

The case usually made for hymns is a bad one. It is that they are old, that they are reverent, and that the modern material is thin — an argument about taste dressed up as an argument about depth, and it convinces nobody under fifty.

The better case is biographical, and it takes an afternoon to check. Go and look at when the ones that lasted were written. It Is Well With My Soul was written by a man crossing the water where his four daughters had drowned a few weeks earlier. Amazing Grace was written by a former slave trader who had come to understand exactly what he had spent his working life doing. William Cowper wrote some of the most durable lines in English hymnody while severely and repeatedly ill in his mind, in years when he believed himself past all help. These are not the odd exception. Go far enough down the list and the pattern is close to a rule.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, and the hymn and heritage repertoire holds its own stretch of the numbers rather than turning up as the occasional older track between two new ones.

Keeping it that way costs something, because the material does not behave. The awkward verse is usually the load-bearing one, and it is the verse everybody wants to cut. A hymn is a sentence somebody had to mean under pressure, and pressure strips out of a line everything that was only ever decorative, which is precisely why it holds weight the next person can lean on. Sand off the difficult verse and what is left is the pleasant half of a document whose whole authority came from the half you removed.

Something has gone quiet in the way new songs are made, and it is nobody’s fault in particular. A great deal of modern worship is written to a deadline, by teams, for a Sunday already in the diary — an honourable way to work that produces perfectly good songs. But there is no mechanism in it for the worst year of somebody’s life. That kind of writing cannot be commissioned or scheduled, and an industry organised around release dates has no way of waiting for it. So it does not wait, and the catalogue fills with songs written in a decent week.

The band is arranged so that a listener can find the register they need by feel — the worship formats together, country and gospel near one another, the hymn and heritage material in its own stretch of the numbers. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about without looking anything up, which is the skill a real dial teaches. A search box can only hand you back the hymn you already knew the name of, and the ones likely to do you good are the ones you have never heard of.
None of this is an argument against new songs, and anybody who turns it into one has misunderstood it. It is an argument about testing.

Be fair to the new material first. It is singable on a first hearing, which hymns frequently are not. It is in the language people actually use, a congregation learns it in a fortnight, and there is nothing holy about an organ. But almost all of it has been written in the major key of a decent year, by people who are well, for people assumed to be well, and none of it has yet been through the only test that counts. A song is not proven when it fills a room; rooms can be filled by production. It is proven when one person in a bad month finds the line still true with the music off.
Nobody knows what a song is worth until somebody has had to sing it on the worst day of their life.

On a Thursday afternoon in a prison chapel there are eleven men, a keyboard slightly out of tune, and a chaplain who has learned not to talk for long. They sing Amazing Grace, because it is the one everybody has, including the two who have not been inside a church since school. A man in his thirties near the back does not sing the first verse at all. He comes in at the second and sings the rest of it flat and loudly, looking at the floor. Afterwards, stacking chairs against the wall, he asks the chaplain whether it is true about the man who wrote it, and what he did for a living, and how long it took him afterwards. The chaplain says it took years. He says right, and carries the last two chairs over.
Nobody had made a case to him. The fact of the writer had been sitting inside the song the entire time, and he found it there himself, in a room he had not chosen to be in.

The honest cost of this repertoire is that a great deal of it is hard work. The words are old and some are genuinely obscure. The tunes were pitched for voices trained in a way almost nobody is trained now. There are hymns that deserved to be forgotten and were not, and there is a real danger of loving the smell of the hymnbook rather than anything printed in it, which is nostalgia and not faith. For somebody unsure they believe any of it, the language is one more locked door.

But the strangeness is not decoration that has aged badly. It is the mark of a sentence written for some purpose other than pleasing you. These lines were not made to be relatable; they were made to be survivable, by people who needed them to hold on the worst day they had had. That is why they sound unlike anything else you will hear this week, and why they are still here when warmer and easier material from the same decades is not.

So the reason the hymns are kept on this band is not heritage and certainly not taste. It is that they are field notes. They are what people wrote down while they were going through it, and kept singing anyway, and left behind in a form durable enough for somebody who does not yet believe a word of it to use. That is rarer than a good tune, and it cannot be manufactured to a schedule.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to assemble, no decision to make before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 309.30 — Gospel Country. It is not the hymnbook, and that is deliberate: it is the tradition that carried on doing the hymnbook’s work after the hymnbook closed. Country gospel is the one popular form left that will still name the trouble out loud — the debt, the drink, the funeral, the marriage that did not hold — and then sing about grace in the same three minutes without flinching at the join. The morning show is Country Gospel Morning and the evening one the Front-Porch Hour, which tells you the posture. Put it on while you are doing something with your hands and wait for a line plainly written by somebody who had been through it. That is the instinct that produced the hymnal in the charity-shop window, still being written this year.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a case. You do not have to settle the argument about old and new to test it, and you do not have to like the organ, because that was never what any of this was about. Put HM 309.30 on for a fortnight while you get on with things. Somewhere in a bad week, months from now, a line you did not set out to learn will already be there when you need it. Somebody wrote it down on the worst day they had, and left it where you would find it without looking.
